video.title: Standard deviation and outliers: How far from the middle?
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello - the students' teacher (main character)
Mr Joseph - the students' maths teacher (cameo)
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to the student (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: Our class and the class next door both had a mean of twelve in the science test. Same number, so same class? No. In our class everyone was close to twelve. In theirs, marks were all over the place.
Today: measuring how spread out data is, and spotting values that do not fit.
The standard deviation is the typical distance of the values from the mean. Small means the values huddle close to the mean. Large means they are spread far away.
To work it out, find each value's distance from the mean, square it, take the mean of the squares, and then the square root. The computer does this in one line. Your job is to read it.
Class A has a standard deviation of about one mark. Class B has about five. The same mean, but class B needs very different help for different pupils.

scenes.on_screen_text: An outlier: far from the rest
scenes.narration: An outlier is a value far from the rest. A height of three hundred centimetres, or a mark of ninety in a test out of twenty. Outliers deserve a closer look before anything else.
One simple rule uses the middle half of the data. Find the quartiles, and the gap between them. Anything more than one and a half gaps beyond the quartiles is flagged as an outlier.

scenes.on_screen_text: What do you do with it?
scenes.narration: Quick check! The register says one pupil took three hundred minutes to get to school. What should you do first?
Check it first. It could be a typing mistake for thirty. Or it could be true, a pupil who walks from a far village. Never delete an outlier just because it is inconvenient.

scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: the middle and the spread
scenes.narration: In the app, open The middle and the spread. Drag one mark far away, and watch how the range and the middle half react differently.
Your turn. Class C has a standard deviation of two, and class D of six. Which class has more mixed marks?
Class D. Remember: the standard deviation is the typical distance from the mean. Outliers are far from the rest. Check them, explain them, and never hide them.
Try it yourself: write down how long your journeys take for a week. Find the values that stand out, and ask: is each one a mistake, or something real?

checkpoints.prompt: The register says one journey took 300 minutes. What should you do first?

options.text: Check whether it is a mistake or true
Replace it with the class mean

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: an outlier might be a typo or a real, important case. Check before you decide.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: never delete an outlier blindly. First check whether it is a mistake.

checkpoints.prompt: Class C has a standard deviation of 2, class D of 6. Which has more mixed marks?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: a larger standard deviation means marks are further from the mean.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: the bigger the standard deviation, the more spread out the marks.
